raw_case_text: A 28-year-old woman was hospitalized for acute-onset high fever, myalgia, arthralgia and ocular pain. Detailed history- taking, hematological and serological investigations established the diagnosis of classic dengue fever (a positive IgM antibody titer); and ruled out mimicking infections like leptospirosis, typhoid, malaria, syphilis, as well as collagen vascular diseases. Seven days later, during the convalescent phase, the patient noticed blurring of the inferior visual field in the right eye. She presented to us two weeks after the ocular symptoms had started. Best corrected visual acuity was 20/20 bilaterally. On slit-lamp examination, anterior segment was unremarkable in both eyes; no anterior vitreous cells or flare was observed. Fundus examination of the right eye showed a patchy area of partially faded retinal whitening in the superotemporal quadrant of the macula, just encroaching into the fovea, with attenuation and sclerosis of the macular division of the superotemporal branch retinal artery [Fig. 1]. The left fundus revealed a single cotton-wool spot towards the edge of the inferotemporal arcade. Midphase fluorescein angiogram of the right eye showed narrowing of the affected arterial segment, blocked background fluorescence in the area of whitening and delayed arteriovenous transit in the affected vessels. Staining and leakage of the occluded artery was observed in the late phase [Fig. 2]. Kinetic central field charting with Bjerrum's screen showed an inferonasal field defect corresponding to the area of arterial occlusion. The patient was referred for a detailed cardiac and carotid evaluation - including carotid doppler study and echocardiography - which was unremarkable. She was followed up for three months. Her visual acuity remained 20/20 in both eyes, but the inferior field defect persisted in the right eye.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 28-year-old female presented with blurring of the inferior visual field in the right eye following an acute febrile illness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient was hospitalized initially for acute-onset high fever, severe myalgia, arthralgia, and retro-ocular pain. Seven days later, during her convalescent period, she developed sudden painless blurring of the inferior visual field of her right eye, presenting for ophthalmic evaluation two weeks after ocular symptom onset.
subjective.past_medical_history: Recent acute febrile illness managed as an inpatient. No prior history of hypertension, thromboembolism, or collagen vascular disorders.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reported inferior visual field blurring in the right eye; preceding illness featured high fever, generalized arthralgias, myalgias, and retro-orbital pain. Denied eye pain at ophthalmic presentation, amaurosis fugax, or motor weakness.

objective.physical_examination: Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes. Slit-lamp biomicroscopy of anterior segments was unremarkable bilaterally without vitreous cells or flare. Right funduscopy revealed a patchy area of partially faded retinal whitening in the superotemporal macular quadrant encroaching on the fovea, with marked attenuation and sclerosis of the macular branch of the superotemporal retinal artery. Left funduscopy revealed an isolated cotton-wool spot near the inferotemporal vascular arcade.
objective.routine_investigations:
Hematologic profile demonstrated transient acute cytopenias and thrombocytopenia during initial febrile hospitalization.
Systemic vascular screening: Transthoracic echocardiogram and bilateral carotid Doppler ultrasound were entirely normal.
objective.advanced_workup:
Fundus fluorescein angiography (FA) of right eye: Mid-phase showed focal arteriolar narrowing, delayed arteriovenous transit, and blocked background choroidal fluorescence in the ischemic zone; late-phase demonstrated hyperfluorescent staining and vascular leakage of the occluded retinal arterial segment.
Visual field examination (Bjerrum screen kinetic perimetry): Demonstrated a dense inferonasal visual field defect corresponding geometrically to the occluded superotemporal macular retinal arteriole.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Branch retinal artery occlusion (BRAO) secondary to Dengue virus infection, confirmed by a positive Dengue IgM antibody titer. Leptospirosis, typhoid fever, malaria, syphilis, systemic lupus erythematosus/collagen vascular diseases, and cardiac/carotid embolic sources were systematically ruled out.
Treatment and outcome: Managed conservatively with observation. Over three months of follow-up, visual acuity remained preserved at 20/20 bilaterally, but the dense right inferonasal visual field defect persisted permanently.
